594: The Coherence-Based Genealogical Method, developed by Gerd Mink, uses computers to compare the full texts of manuscripts and map how readings likely passed from one text to another. It led to 34 changes in the Catholic Letters in NA28.
595: Instead of grouping manuscripts into broad text-types, the CBGM compares every manuscript's text at every place, then asks which texts are 'potential ancestors' of others. Editors still make judgements, but the method makes them more testable and consistent. It was first applied in the *Editio Critica Maior* of the Catholic Letters (second edition 2013) and then to Acts and Mark. The result has been a slightly greater respect for some Byzantine readings and more places marked as uncertain (with a diamond sign). Critics say it relies heavily on editors' initial decisions and treats texts, not physical manuscripts.
598: Some earlier proposals of a Hellenistic date, now largely abandoned
601: A shortened form of the priestly blessing and phrases describing God as one who keeps covenant and drives away evil.
603: 1979, by Gabriel Barkay's excavation in a burial cave opposite Mount Zion
604: The oldest known artefacts carrying words closely matching a biblical text, from the time of Judah's last kings. They show the blessing in use before the exile, and how ordinary people wore sacred words as protection.
609: The Ten Commandments (mixing features of Exodus 20 and Deuteronomy 5) followed by the Shema.
611: Bought in Egypt by W. L. Nash, published 1903
612: Before 1947 the oldest known Hebrew biblical text. Its form agrees with some Septuagint readings, showing that pre-Masoretic Hebrew texts sometimes differed in small ways.
616: Parchment scroll, 17 sheets sewn together, about 7.3 metres long
617: All 66 chapters of Isaiah, complete apart from small damaged spots.
618: Shrine of the Book, Israel Museum, Jerusalem
620: About a thousand years older than the medieval Hebrew codices, yet its text is substantially the same as the Masoretic Isaiah, differing mainly in spelling and small details. A few readings (for example 'he will see light' in Isa 53:11, shared with the Septuagint) have been adopted by many modern translations. It is a showcase for both the stability and the small variety of the Hebrew text.
625: Israel Antiquities Authority / Rockefeller Museum, Jerusalem
627: Often agrees with the Septuagint and Chronicles against the Masoretic text of Samuel, which has many copying slips. It preserves a paragraph about Nahash the Ammonite before 1 Sam 11 that the NRSV added to its text.
630: Roberts' original estimate (first half of 2nd century)
633: Papyrus codex fragment, about the size of a credit card
634: A few words from John 18:31-33 on one side and John 18:37-38 on the other.
636: Bought in Egypt by Bernard Grenfell in 1920; identified by C. H. Roberts in 1934
637: Usually cited as the earliest New Testament fragment. If the earlier date is right, it shows John's Gospel was being copied in Egypt within decades of its writing, which helped end 19th-century theories dating John to the late 2nd century. Because it is a codex (written on both sides), it also shows early Christian use of the book form.
643: Letters of Paul: Romans (part), Hebrews, 1-2 Corinthians, Ephesians, Galatians, Philippians, Colossians, 1 Thessalonians (part). Leaves at each end are lost.
644: Chester Beatty Library, Dublin, and University of Michigan, Ann Arbor
645: Acquired in the early 1930s from Egypt
646: The oldest substantial collection of Paul's letters. It places Hebrews right after Romans, showing that early Egyptian Christians counted Hebrews as Pauline. It lacks 'in Ephesus' at Eph 1:1 and places the Romans doxology after chapter 15. A very early date around AD 85 was proposed by Kim but is rejected by most.
651: Most of John's Gospel (chapters 1-14 largely complete, fragments of the rest).
652: Bodmer Library, Cologny (Geneva), and Chester Beatty Library
653: Acquired in the 1950s from Egypt; published 1956
654: One of the oldest near-complete Gospel books. The scribe made many mistakes and corrected many of them, giving a rare look at copying and correcting in action. It lacks John 7:53-8:11.
661: Acquired by Martin Bodmer in the 1950s; published 1961
662: Its text is extremely close to Codex Vaticanus, showing that this careful text existed long before the 4th century. It contains the earliest copy of the Lord's Prayer in Luke, and lacks Luke 22:43-44 and Luke 23:34a.
664: P45, P46, P47 (and Old Testament codices)
666: P45: the four Gospels and Acts (damaged); P46: Paul's letters; P47: Revelation 9-17. Also Greek Old Testament books (Genesis, Numbers, Deuteronomy, Isaiah, Jeremiah, Ezekiel, Daniel, Esther and others).
667: Chester Beatty Library, Dublin (part of P46 in Michigan)
668: Bought by Alfred Chester Beatty from dealers; announced 1931
669: P45 is among the earliest examples of the four Gospels and Acts bound in one book, evidence that the fourfold Gospel collection was being produced as a unit. Together the papyri show a range of 2nd-3rd century text forms in Egypt.
674: Parchment codex, three columns per page
675: Most of the Greek Old Testament (Septuagint) and the New Testament up to Hebrews 9:14; the rest of Hebrews, the Pastoral Letters, Philemon and Revelation are lost (later replaced in a medieval hand).
676: Vatican Library, Rome (recorded in its catalogue since 1475)
677: Never 'discovered'; long held by the Vatican, but access was restricted until the 19th century
678: Often considered the single most important manuscript of the Greek New Testament. It ends Mark at 16:8, leaving a blank column, and lacks John 7:53-8:11. Its marginal signs (distigmai) may mark known variant points, a subject of study.
682: Parchment codex, four columns per page
683: Much of the Septuagint, the complete New Testament (the oldest complete one), plus the *Epistle of Barnabas* and part of the *Shepherd of Hermas*.
684: British Library (most), with parts at Leipzig University Library, the National Library of Russia and St Catherine's Monastery
685: Brought to Europe by Constantin von Tischendorf, 1844 and 1859; further leaves found at Sinai in 1975
686: Oldest complete New Testament. It ends Mark at 16:8 and lacks the woman taken in adultery. It was corrected by many later hands over centuries, which lets scholars watch the text being adjusted. Including Barnabas and Hermas shows that the edge of the canon was still somewhat flexible in the 4th century. Fully online since 2009.
692: The Gospels (in the 'Western' order Matthew, John, Luke, Mark), Acts, and a fragment of 3 John.
693: Given to Cambridge in 1581 by the reformer Theodore Beza, who obtained it after the sack of Lyon in 1562
694: The chief Greek witness to the 'Western' text, which has many additions and rewordings; its Acts is nearly 10 percent longer than the usual text. It is the oldest Greek manuscript containing John 7:53-8:11 and includes a unique saying about a man working on the Sabbath after Luke 6:4.
697: The four Gospels in the Western order.
698: Freer Gallery of Art, Smithsonian Institution, Washington, D.C.
699: Bought by Charles Lang Freer in Egypt in 1906
700: Its text changes type from section to section, as if copied from several sources. In Mark 16 it contains the 'Freer Logion', a unique addition after verse 14 in which the disciples excuse their unbelief and Jesus replies, evidence of how the longer ending was itself expanded.
704: Nearly the whole Bible (with some losses in Matthew, John and 2 Corinthians), plus *1 and 2 Clement* and, in its table of contents, the *Psalms of Solomon*.
706: Given to King Charles I in 1627 by Cyril Lucaris, Patriarch of Constantinople
707: The first of the great early codices available to Western scholars, arriving just too late for the KJV. Its Gospels mostly follow the Byzantine type, while its letters and Revelation follow the older Alexandrian type, and it is one of the best witnesses for Revelation.
711: Parts of the Old Testament and parts of every New Testament book except 2 Thessalonians and 2 John.
713: In the 12th century its Bible text was scraped off and overwritten with sermons of Ephrem the Syrian; Tischendorf deciphered the underlying text in 1840-1843
714: A key example of a palimpsest. Its mixed text is important for the New Testament, and modern imaging continues to recover readings.
719: Old and New Testament in Syriac; the earliest dated manuscript (British Library Add. 14,425, AD 463/464) contains parts of the Pentateuch. Codex Ambrosianus (Milan, 6th-7th century) has the whole Old Testament.
720: British Library, Biblioteca Ambrosiana (Milan) and others
721: Many reached the British Museum in the 1840s from the Monastery of the Syrians in the Egyptian desert
722: Among the oldest dated Bible manuscripts in any language. The Peshitta is still the Bible of Syriac churches, and it witnesses to both Hebrew and Greek texts from an early date.
725: Purple-dyed parchment with silver and gold ink
726: Parts of the four Gospels in Ulfilas' Gothic translation.
728: Found at the abbey of Werden in the 16th century; taken by Swedish troops from Prague in 1648
729: The main surviving witness to the Gothic Bible and the oldest substantial text in a Germanic language; probably made for the Ostrogothic court in Italy.
733: Parchment, over 1,000 leaves; the hides of perhaps 500 calves
734: The complete Latin Bible in a single volume.
736: Made at Wearmouth-Jarrow, England; its English origin was proved in the 1880s
737: The oldest surviving complete Vulgate and one of the best witnesses to Jerome's text; used for the modern critical Vulgate editions.
740: Hebrew (with Masoretic vowels, accents and notes)
741: Originally the whole Hebrew Bible; today about 60 percent survives (most of the Torah is missing).
742: Israel Museum (Shrine of the Book), Jerusalem
743: Kept in the Aleppo synagogue for centuries; damaged in 1947; brought to Israel by 1958
744: The most authoritative Masoretic manuscript, pointed by Aaron ben Asher, and praised by Maimonides. Base text of the Hebrew University Bible and the Jerusalem Crown edition.
748: The complete Hebrew Bible, with decorated 'carpet pages'.
749: National Library of Russia, St Petersburg
750: Acquired by the collector Abraham Firkovich in the 19th century; came to the imperial library in 1863
751: The oldest complete Hebrew Bible, and the base of *Biblia Hebraica Stuttgartensia* and *Biblia Hebraica Quinta*, so it stands behind the Old Testament of nearly every modern translation.
753: Did Mark's Gospel originally stop at 16:8, with frightened women fleeing the empty tomb, or did it include the twelve verses of resurrection appearances, the great commission, snake-handling and drinking poison?
754: The verses appear in the vast majority of Greek manuscripts (including Alexandrinus, Ephraemi, Bezae and Washingtonianus), and in most Latin, Syriac and Coptic versions. Irenaeus (around 180) quotes Mark 16:19 as part of Mark (*Against Heresies* 3.10.5), and Tatian's *Diatessaron* appears to use the ending, so it was known in the 2nd century. Some argue an ending at 'for they were afraid' is too abrupt for a book.
755: The two oldest complete manuscripts, Sinaiticus and Vaticanus, end at 16:8 (Vaticanus leaves a blank column). Eusebius and Jerome say the most accurate copies they knew ended there. Other manuscripts have a different 'shorter ending', some have both, and one (Washingtonianus) adds more. The vocabulary and style differ noticeably from Mark, and the passage reads like a summary of appearances in the other Gospels and Acts. Most scholars think it was added in the early 2nd century; they debate whether Mark meant to end at 16:8 or the original ending was lost.
756: Most modern translations (NIV, ESV, NRSV, CSB, NASB) print it with brackets or a note saying the earliest manuscripts lack it. The KJV and NKJV print it as normal text (the NKJV with a note). Some put the shorter ending too.
757: It is the longest disputed passage in the New Testament, but no core belief depends on it: the resurrection is announced in Mark 16:6, and the appearances are told in the other Gospels. Practices such as snake-handling in a few churches have rested on 16:18.
759: Was the story of Jesus saying 'let him who is without sin cast the first stone' originally part of John's Gospel?
760: It appears in most later Greek manuscripts and in Jerome's Vulgate; Jerome says it was found in many Greek and Latin copies. Codex Bezae (around 400) contains it. A similar story is mentioned in the 3rd-century *Didascalia* and possibly by Papias (according to Eusebius). Augustine suggested some had removed it fearing it would encourage adultery. Many scholars think it is an authentic early tradition about Jesus, even if not originally in John.
761: It is missing from the earliest manuscripts (P66, P75, Sinaiticus, Vaticanus, and probably Alexandrinus and Ephraemi, judging by space), from early Syriac and Coptic versions, and no Greek church writer comments on it in John before the 12th century. In manuscripts that include it, it 'floats': after John 7:36, 7:44, 21:25, or after Luke 21:38. Its style is more like Luke's than John's, and it interrupts the flow from 7:52 to 8:12.
762: Most modern translations bracket it with a note that the earliest manuscripts lack it; some put it at the end of John. The KJV and NKJV print it in place.
763: Its message about mercy and judgement fits Jesus' teaching elsewhere, so many churches still read it. The question is whether it belongs to John's text, not whether Jesus could have acted this way.
764: The Comma Johanneum ('these three are one')
765: The KJV reads 'For there are three that bear record in heaven, the Father, the Word, and the Holy Ghost: and these three are one.' Is this in the original letter?
766: The words appear in the later Latin Vulgate tradition and were cited in Latin from around the 4th or 5th century (first clearly in the *Liber Apologeticus* attributed to Priscillian, around 380). Some argue Cyprian (around 250) alludes to it, though he may be interpreting the 'three witnesses' of verse 8 symbolically. Defenders of the Textus Receptus argue that it was dropped from Greek copies and that the grammar of verse 8 reads more smoothly with it.
767: It is absent from every Greek manuscript before about the 14th century; it appears in only about ten late Greek manuscripts, several only in the margin and some translated from Latin. No Greek writer quotes it during the Trinitarian debates of the 4th century, when it would have been very useful. It is absent from early Latin, Syriac, Coptic and other versions. Erasmus left it out of his first two editions and added it in the third (1522) after a Greek manuscript containing it (Codex Montfortianus, likely made around 1520) was produced.
768: Almost all modern translations omit it from the text, many with a footnote. The KJV and NKJV include it (the NKJV with a note).
769: It is the clearest Trinitarian statement in the KJV, but the doctrine of the Trinity was formulated in the 4th century without it and rests on many other passages. Nearly all scholars, conservative and liberal, regard it as a later addition, probably a margin comment that entered the text.
770: The angel and the sweat like drops of blood
771: Did Luke write that an angel strengthened Jesus in Gethsemane and that his sweat became like great drops of blood?
772: Found in the original hand of Sinaiticus, in Bezae, and in many later manuscripts. Justin Martyr (around 155), Irenaeus and Hippolytus know the tradition of the bloody sweat, so it is very early. Some argue it was removed by scribes uncomfortable with Jesus appearing weak and needing an angel's help.
773: Absent from P75 (around 200), Vaticanus, Alexandrinus, Washingtonianus and others; some manuscripts mark it as doubtful; some place it in Matthew instead. Bart Ehrman and others think it was added to stress Jesus' real human suffering against docetists (who said he only seemed human). Others argue that the passage breaks the careful structure of Luke 22:39-46.
774: NA28 prints it in double brackets (likely not original but very old). The ESV, NIV and NASB print it with a note; the NRSV prints it in brackets. Scholarly opinion is genuinely split.
775: It shapes the picture of Jesus' agony. Even without it, Jesus' distress is clear in Mark 14:33-36 and Heb 5:7.
777: Did Luke record Jesus praying from the cross, 'Father, forgive them, for they know not what they do'?
778: Present in the original hand of Sinaiticus, in Alexandrinus, Ephraemi, and most manuscripts; known in the 2nd century (Irenaeus, the *Diatessaron*). It matches Luke's themes of forgiveness and is echoed by Stephen's prayer in Acts. Some suggest scribes removed it after the fall of Jerusalem in 70, when it seemed God had not forgiven the Jews, or out of anti-Jewish feeling.
779: Absent from P75, Vaticanus, the first hand of Bezae, Washingtonianus and some early versions. A deliberate omission of such a beloved saying is hard to explain, which leads some to think it was a genuine tradition added from oral memory.
780: NA28 puts it in double brackets; most English translations print it, sometimes with a note that some early manuscripts lack it.
781: One of the most quoted words of Jesus. Many scholars who doubt it was originally in Luke still think it may preserve a real saying.
783: Before his baptism, did the Ethiopian official say, 'I believe that Jesus Christ is the Son of God'?
784: Irenaeus (around 180) cites the confession (*Against Heresies* 3.12.8), so it is old. It appears in Codex Laudianus (E, 6th century), many Latin manuscripts and a minority of Greek ones; Erasmus included it from the Latin tradition.
785: Absent from P45, P74, Sinaiticus, Vaticanus, Alexandrinus, Ephraemi and most Greek manuscripts including the Byzantine majority. It looks like a baptismal formula added to show that faith was confessed before baptism.
786: Omitted or footnoted in most modern translations (which is why verse 37 seems 'missing'); included in the KJV and NKJV.
787: Its absence does not change the story; it simply reflects early church baptism practice. It is often cited in debates about 'missing verses' in modern Bibles.
788: 'For thine is the kingdom, and the power, and the glory'
789: Did Jesus' model prayer in Matthew end with this doxology (praise formula)?
790: Found in most later Greek manuscripts (including Washingtonianus) and some early versions. The *Didache* (around 100) gives the prayer with a two-part ending ('for yours is the power and the glory forever'), showing that some kind of closing was used in worship very early. Jewish prayers commonly ended with praise, and 1 Chr 29:11 contains similar words.
791: Absent from Sinaiticus, Vaticanus, Bezae, early Latin versions, and the commentaries of Origen, Tertullian and Cyprian on the prayer. It appears in several different forms, a typical sign of a liturgical addition. Luke's version of the prayer has no doxology.
792: Most modern translations put it in a footnote; the KJV and NKJV include it. Protestant churches usually say it; the Catholic Mass says a version after a separate prayer.
793: A clear example of worship practice entering the text. Its words are biblical in spirit and drawn from 1 Chronicles, so the issue is placement, not doctrine.
794: The angel stirring the pool of Bethesda
795: Did John explain that sick people waited because an angel stirred the water, and the first one in was healed?
796: Verse 4 is in Alexandrinus and most later manuscripts; Tertullian (*On Baptism* 5) knows of the angel, so the tradition is early. The sick man's words in John 5:7 assume the water was stirred, and some argue the explanation was dropped because it sounded superstitious.
797: Absent from P66, P75, Sinaiticus, Vaticanus, the first hand of Ephraemi and others. Many manuscripts that include it mark it with asterisks or obeli (doubt signs), and its wording varies a lot, with several words not used elsewhere by John. It looks like an explanatory note of local belief.
798: Most modern translations omit verse 4 (and the end of verse 3) in the text with a note; the KJV and NKJV include them.
799: The healing story itself is unaffected; the difference is whether John endorses the angel explanation or simply reports what people believed.
800: The repeated grace blessing in Romans 16
801: Is 'The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with you all. Amen' original at Romans 16:24, and where did Romans originally end?
802: Found in Bezae, the Western tradition and most later manuscripts; some place it after 16:27 instead.
803: Absent from P46, P61, Sinaiticus, Vaticanus, Alexandrinus and Ephraemi. It duplicates 16:20. More broadly, the closing doxology (16:25-27) moves around in manuscripts: after 14:23, after 15:33 (P46), after 16:23, in two places, or nowhere. This suggests shorter editions of Romans circulated, possibly one associated with Marcion ending at chapter 14.
804: Most modern translations omit 16:24 with a note; the KJV and NKJV include it.
805: Minor in content, but the wandering doxology is important evidence about how Paul's letters were collected and edited in the earliest period.
806: 'Let your women keep silence': where does it belong?
807: No manuscript leaves out these two verses, but some place them after verse 40. Does this suggest they were a margin note added to the text?
808: That they are original: every surviving manuscript contains them, and most scholars (for example D. A. Carson, Anthony Thiselton, and many complementarian and egalitarian scholars alike) accept them as Paul's, explaining the Western placement as a scribe's rearrangement for smoother flow. Interpreters then debate what kind of speech is restricted (disruptive questions, judging prophecies, or speaking in general).
809: That they were a later insertion: Gordon Fee and Philip Payne argue that the floating position (in Bezae, other Western manuscripts and Ambrosiaster after 14:40) is the typical sign of a margin gloss; that the verses seem to clash with 1 Cor 11:5, where women pray and prophesy; and that marks in Vaticanus (distigmai) and a note in Codex Fuldensis may flag a known problem. Critics reply that the Vaticanus marks' meaning and date are disputed and that the clash can be explained.
810: All major translations print the verses in the usual place; some (NRSV, NET) mention the placement issue in notes. Many interpret the passage in context rather than as a later addition.
811: It bears directly on the debate about women's roles in church. A textual question here should not be used to settle the theological question, and both sides of that debate include scholars who accept the verses as original.
812: 'The Son of God' in Mark's opening line
813: Does Mark open with 'The beginning of the gospel of Jesus Christ, the Son of God', or just 'of Jesus Christ'?
